text:
Ontario

Supreme Court

David v. Congregation B’Nai
Israel
,

Date: 1999-04-12

Joseph Ben David,
Plaintiff

and

Congregation B’Nai
Israel
, Defendant

Ontario
Court of Justice, General Division

Festeryga J.

Heard: November
16-18, 1998

Judgment:
April 12, 1999
[1]

Docket:
St. Catharines
37158/96

Brian A. Grosman, Q.C. and John R.
Martin, for Plaintiff.

William E. Donegan, for Defendant.

Festeryga J.:

1. Procedural Consent Matters

1
The parties agreed that the plaintiff will not
proceed with paragraphs 1 (a), (b) and (d) and accordingly will not be relying
on paragraphs 11, 12, 16, 17, 19, 20 and 21 (a) and (b) of the Statement of
Claim.

2
It is further agreed that it will not be
necessary to argue paragraph 6 of the Statement of Defence and the defendants
will not pursue paragraph 7 of the Statement of Defence wherein they allege
that the plaintiff’s employment was terminated for cause.

3
It was further agreed that paragraph 1(c) of
the plaintiff’s Statement of Claim may be amended to read $110,000.00 instead
of $85,000.00 and paragraph 18 of the Statement of Claim may be amended to
change the number of months in the last line of that paragraph to read 21
months instead of 15 months notice.

4
The parties have agreed that the plaintiff
will be seeking a total of 30 months notice made up of nine months working
notice and an additional 21 months.

5
Order to go accordingly.

2. Introduction

6
The plaintiff, is 62 years of age, married
with five children. He came to St. Catharines in about 1969. Prior to coming to St. Catharines he was a supply Teacher at a Jewish school in Toronto and before that he taught at a
Jewish school in Casablanca,
Morocco.

7
In May of 1969 he was offered a position by
the defendant and on the 12th of June, 1969, he signed his first agreement with the defendant to work as a
Teacher and Chazan (Cantor).

8
He eventually progressed to the point where he
was Assistant Rabbi as well as a Teacher and a Cantor. At the encouragement of
the defendant he obtained his “
Smicha
”.

This means that he became
a fully ordained Rabbi according to Jewish law. As set out at Tab 14 of Exhibit
1, on Sunday, September 10th, 1989, the defendant congregation gathered to
honour the plaintiff and his wife to celebrate their 20th anniversary of
service to the community and to announce that the plaintiff would be designated
the congregation’s spiritual leader and Rabbi.

9

Documents were signed from time to time
by the parties, the last being dated September 1st, 1994.

10
In November of 1994, the plaintiff was given
written notice that the congregation would not be renewing the last contract at
the expiration of its term. The letter at Tab 26, Exhibit 1, sets out the date
August 31st, 1994. That must be a typographical error because paragraph 2 of
the contract sets a conclusion date of August 31st, 1995. The plaintiff was
shocked by this for many reasons which will be referred to later. It never
occurred to him that any of the documents that he signed set out fixed terms
and provisions for notice of renewal or non‑renewal of his employment. He
signed the contracts as they were presented to him. His prime concern was the
amount of the remuneration. He never expected that the defendant would do
anything to compromise his position as the Rabbi and spiritual leader of the
congregation. He therefore takes the position that he was an employee with an
indefinite term and entitled to reasonable notice.

11
On the other hand the defendant relies on the
documents and in particular the most recent one and say that they are entitled
to give him notice that they would not renew the agreement.

12
The plaintiff therefore brings this action
for wrongful dismissal and asks for 30 months notice total which would include
the nine months working notice and he also asks for punitive damages.

13
In the Statement of Defence the defendant
alleged cause and agreed to provide particulars, which they did, as set out at
pages 21 and 22 of the Trial Record. These allegations for cause came as a
complete surprise to the plaintiff because he alleges that none of these complaints
were brought to his attention while in the employ of the defendant. He was
provided with a glowing letter of recommendation as set out in Tab 28 of
Exhibit 1. These allegations of cause continued until they were withdrawn
shortly before trial.

3. Issues

14
1. Is the agreement between the parties dated
September 1st, 1994, found at Tab 23 of Exhibit 1, a legally enforceable
contract?

2. In the event that the said agreement is not
legally enforceable,

(a) what is the plaintiff’s entitlement to
reasonable notice at common law?

(b) what are the plaintiffs damages for
wrongful dismissal?

(c) should the plaintiff’s damages for
wrongful dismissal be reduced on the basis that he failed to mitigate his
damages?

3. Should the plaintiff be awarded punitive
damages, and if so in what amount?

4. The “Agreements”

15
By letter dated May 16th, 1969, from Jack Silverstein,
Chairman of the Board of Education of the defendant, the defendant stated that
the Committee has agreed to engage the plaintiff for the congregation under the
conditions discussed. It promised that a contract would be forwarded to the
plaintiff shortly.

16
There is no evidence as to what conditions
were discussed. Jack Silverstein did not come forward to give evidence on
behalf of the Board of Education.

17
The document at Exhibit 1, Tab 1 (a) is an
agreement made in duplicate on the 12th of June, 1969. It is signed by the
parties but not witnessed.

18
It provides that the defendant agrees to
employ the plaintiff as a Teacher and Cantor for a term of one year commencing
September 1st, 1969, and from thenceforth next ensuing to be fully completed
and ended on the 31st day of August, 1970.I find that there was no discussion
between the parties with respect to this limited engagement and I also find
that the plaintiff did not agree to a one year term. I find that the plaintiff
was concerned about the remuneration and that he was looking for a long term
commitment.

19
The remuneration was for $5,000.00 plus an
additional $1,500.00 for living accommodations and $1,000.00 for library and
other expenses.

20
There is an option to renew in paragraph 9 in
favour of the defendant provided that the defendant gives the plaintiff written
notice not later than 60 days prior to the expiration of the agreement. There
is no evidence that this was explained to the plaintiff before he signed it. He
was unaware of the stringent and onerous provisions of the fixed term and
renewal clauses. The defendant unilaterally included those clauses in the
agreement.

21
I find that there was no written notice to
renew as required by the document.

22
I find that there was no document presented
for the period September 1st, 1970 to August 31, 1971 and therefore find that the plaintiff worked
without any written agreement for that period of time.

23
At Tab 2 of Exhibit 1 we have an agreement
dated the 23rd of June, 1971.
It is not signed. It is for the term September 1st, 1971 to August 31st, 1972. The remuneration is $16,000.00
per year plus $1,500.00 for living expenses and $1,500.00 for travel, library
and other expenses. There is an option to renew in favour of the defendant upon
the latter giving the plaintiff 60 days written notice prior to the expiration.
The evidence is unsatisfactory as to whether this document was ever signed. I
find that on the balance of probabilities it was not signed and that the
plaintiff continued to work without a written contract.

24
I find that no written notice was given by
the defendant to the plaintiff to renew his services as required by the latter
document.

25
The next written agreement is at Exhibit 1,
Tab 3. It is dated the 29th of July, 1975 for the period September 1st, 1975 to August 31st, 1977. There
was no written agreement for the period August 31, 1970 to September 1st, 1975. The
agreement at Tab 3 is for a two year period. It is signed and witnessed. The
plaintiff is again employed as a Teacherand a Cantor. The remuneration is
$10,600.00 plus $1,500.00 for living accommodations and an additional $1,500.00
for transportation, library and other expenses for the first term. For the
second term the remuneration is $11,800.00 plus the $1,500.00 and $1,500.00. In
this agreement there is no provision for renewal. The agreement contemplates
that at the end of the two years the job would be fully completed.

26
I find that the plaintiff probably read the
agreement but did not understand it, especially the two year term that was
never explained to him and it was never explained to him that there was no
option to renew. He, as in the other agreements that he signed with the
defendant, relied completely on the defendant to treat him fairly.

27
The next agreement is at Tab 4. It is dated the 2nd of May, 1977. It is signed and witnessed
and for the purported period of two years from the 1st of September, 1977 to the 31st of August, 1979. The plaintiff was again
employed as a Teacher and a Cantor.

28
There is no provision for a renewal.

29
The remuneration is $12,500.00 for each year
until August 31st, 1979 plus an additional $1,750.00 for living accommodations
and a similar amount for transportation, library and other expenses in each
year.

30
There is no renewal clause.

31
There is no agreement for the period August 31st, 1979 to September 1st, 1981 and
therefore I find that the plaintiff carried on his duties without a written
agreement during that period of time.

32
The next agreement is at Tab 5. It is not
legible to a great extent. It is dated the blank day of blank, 1981. It is
signed but not witnessed and at page 27 of Exhibit 1 at clause 3 (a) it would
appear to be for the period September 1st, 1981 to August 31st, 1983. The remuneration is not clear from the
document.

33
There is no renewal clause.

34
By this stage the plaintiff had progressed to
Assistant Rabbi although not fully ordained as well as being a Teacher and a
Cantor.

35
At Tab 6 we have an agreement dated September 1st, 1983. It is signed by all parties
but not witnessed and purports to be for a period of two years, commencing
September 1st, 1983 and completed on the 31st of August, 1985.

36
There is no renewal clause.

37
The remuneration is $17,400.00 for the first
year plus an allowance of $5,500.00 and $18,100.00 for the second year with an
allowance of $6,000.00.

38
In that agreement the defendant hired the
plaintiff to be an Assistant Rabbi, Teacher and a Cantor.

39
It is the recollection of the plaintiff that
all of the agreements that were signed and any agreements that exist were
signed after he began working in his various capacities. I accept that
evidence.

40
We next have an agreement at Tab 9 of Exhibit
1 which is dated the 1st of September, 1985. It is signed by all parties but
not witnessed. It purports to be for a two year period commencing September 1st, 1985 and completed and ended on
the 31st of August, 1987.

41
There is no renewal clause.

42
The plaintiff is described as an Assistant
Rabbi, Teacher and a Cantor.

43
The remuneration is $19,600.00 plus $8,400.00
over the first 12 months and $21,000.00 plus $9,000.00 over the second 12
months.

44
There is no written agreement for the period August 31st, 1987 to the 1st day of September,
1989. The defendant did not terminate the plaintiff during that period of time.

45
I am satisfied that the defendant had such
confidence in the work and ability of the plaintiff that they encouraged him to
become a fully ordained Rabbi and an agreement was prepared by the defendant,
found at Tab 10

(a). It is not dated. It is signed by all
parties. In this agreement the plaintiff is a Rabbi and he was expected to
serve as the spiritual leader of the congregation. He was also employed at that
time as the Principal of the Hebrew school responsible for the operation and
organization of the education and adult education and serve as advisor to the
leaders of the various youth groups of the congregation. He was required to
teach annually not less than two grades in the Hebrew School, Hebrew High
School and Bar and Bat Mitzvah classes, all at the
direction of the Board of Education of the Synagogue. His further duties
included assistance in the Cantorial portion of the High Holidays services.

46
Included in the agreement was a term of two
years commencing the 1st of September, 1989 and concluding the 31st of August, 1991 with a remuneration of
$65,000.00 per annum.

47
The agreement provided for notice by either
party not less than six months prior to the termination of the term, that is,
six months prior to the 31st of August, 1991 of either party’s intention with
respect to the renewal of the contract of employment. If both parties wished to
renew then the terms would be the subject of a separate and new agreement.

48
If there was not to be a renewal then the
plaintiff would be allowed sufficient time during the last six months of his
agreement to seek alternative employment provided that such would not
unreasonably interfere with the performance of the obligations of Rabbi as
provided in the agreement.

49
We next move to Tab 18 which is an agreement
dated the 2nd of September, 1991. It is signed on behalf of both parties but there is no date above
the signatures. It purports to be for the term of one year commencing the 1st
of September, 1991, and concluding on the 31st of August, 1992. The renewal
clause is similar to the previous agreement at Tab 10 (a) except that the
notice period is reduced from six months to three months and the time allowed
to the Rabbi to seek alternative employment is reduced from six months to three
months.

50
The remuneration remains at $65,000.00 a
year. The duties remain the same.

51
The next agreement is at Tab 19 of Exhibit 1.
It has a typed in date of 1st of September, 1992, but it has no date when the
parties executed the agreement although it was signed by both parties. It
purports to be for a term of one year from the 1st of September, 1992, to the
31 st of August, 1993. The duties are the same. The remuneration is $65,000.00
plus a sum not to exceed $2,200.00 for extended health care benefits. The
notice with respect to renewal is moved back up to six months prior to the
termination but for some unexplained reason the time that the Rabbi would be
given to seek alternative employment is three months rather than six months.

52
Moving on to Exhibit 1, Tab 20, we have an
agreement dated the 1st of September, 1993. It is signed but there is no date of execution. The purported term
of employment is for one year from the 1st of September, 1993 to August 31, 1994. The renewal notice is six months
and the Rabbi would be given three months to find a new job. The remuneration
is the same as the previous agreement and there is a new provision saying that
the defendant would have no obligation to ensure retirement benefits and that
the Rabbi acknowledges that provision for the same as his own responsibility.

53
We next come to agreements at Tabs 23 and 23
A of Exhibit 1. They are dated the 1st of September, 1994, on a typewritten
form. The agreement at Tab 23, is signed by both parties but a date is not
inserted above the signatures. At 23A it is signed only by Ronald S. Williams
and that has a date of 11th July, 1994. It is not signed by the plaintiff. I accept that this was the
plaintiff’s copy. Paragraph 3 of the agreement purports to be for a term of one
year commencing the 1st of September, 1994 and concluding on the 31st of August, 1995. The duties remain the
same. The remuneration remains the same and there is a renewal clause requiring
six months notice and allowing the Rabbi three months of notice to relocate.

54
At Tab 26 there is a letter dated November
21, 1994, from Ronald S. Williams, Chairman of the Board of Governors, giving
the plaintiff notice that the defendant will not be renewing his contract at
the expiration of its present term. I understand that to mean August, 31, 1995. I find that this was the first
time that the defendant ever gave the plaintiff notice, either written or oral,
of its intention of either renewing or not renewing any one of the contracts
according to its term. Certainly the plaintiff never did give notice of his
intention not to renew any of the agreements that he had with the defendant and
expected that his employment, subject to reasonable notice, would be for an
indefinite period.

55
With respect to all of the agreements that
the plaintiff signed, I find that it was never his intention to be employed for
a limited term. I find that the amount of remuneration was to be renegotiated
from time to time but that he was to be employed in the long term.

5. Assurances

56
There was conduct by the defendant that in my
view led the plaintiff to believe that his employment was long term and not for
a fixed term as relied upon by the defendant. The facts are as follows.

57
No notice of renewal of an agreement was ever
given to the plaintiff by the defendant except for the last notice.

58
The agreements were presented in a manner
that leads me to the conclusion that these were not important documents to be
relied upon. Some documents were signed and others were not. There were times
the plaintiff worked without a document having been signed. Documents were
presented to the plaintiff while at school when he was otherwise occupied.

59
Exhibit 1, Tab 17 is a letter dated September
25, 1991, from R.S. Williams enclosing a contract. He writes “
much of the
contract is identical or similar to your previous agreement
”,

as if
to say it is a
pro forma
agreement, the usual sort of thing, not to be
taken seriously. Mr. Williams, a lawyer, did not take it seriously because
he did not notice the reduction of the two year term to the one year term in
the previous contract.

60
At Exhibit 1, Tab 7, in a letter dated July 12th, 1984, Harold Nash, President of the
Board of Governors, refers to a unanimous resolution of the Board. The
plaintiff is assured that the Board wanted the plaintiff to continue as long as
he cared to. This was at a time when the plaintiff was having serious problems
with his voice. This assurance, in my view, supports the plaintiffs position
that it was a long term relationship rather than for a fixed term.

61
As further assurance of a long term
relationship, the Board convinced the plaintiff to continue his education to
become an ordained Rabbi. See the proposal, Exhibit 1, Tab 10. In that document
an offer is made by the Congregation of enthusiastic support of the Board of
Governors, particularly the strong support of individual committee chairmen. To
further bolster the belief of the plaintiff that the Board was supporting him,
I refer to Exhibit 1, Tab 14, which is evidence of an announcement of the
celebration to honour the plaintiff and his wife.

6. Analysis

62
A. Is the agreement between the parties dated
September 1st, 1994, found at Tab 23 of Exhibit 1, a legally enforceable
contract?

63
My answer is no. I must consider this
document in light of what preceded it.

64
As set out earlier there were many agreements
which, in my view, were not considered as serious documents to be relied upon
by the parties. The plaintiff worked sometimes without a document. At times he
worked with a document that was prepared but it was not signed by the parties.

65
The plaintiff was never told and was not
aware of a fixed term. This fixed term was never explained to him.

66
On the balance of probabilities the fixed
terms were put into the documents after the plaintiff had conducted salary
discussions with the defendant and without any further consideration.

67
The plaintiff had complete trust in the
defendant that he would be dealt with fairly. He had good reason to believe
that because of the assurances given to him and the faith the defendant had in
him.

68
B. In the event that this Honourable Court
determines that the September 1st, 1994 agreement is not legally enforceable,

(i) What is the plaintiff’s entitlement to
reasonable notice at common law?

69
I will first apply the factors to be
considered as set out in
Bardai v. Globe & Mail Ltd.
(1960),
1960 CanLII 294 (ON HCJ)
, 24
D.L.R. (2d) 140 (Ont. H.C.).

70
The character of the plaintiff’s employment
is, in my view, special. It is so because he was responsible for the spiritual
and educational lives of the Congregation. He had to prepare the children for
significant times in their lives, taught school and acted as principal. He
acted as Cantor and Assistant Rabbi and in the end as Rabbi. All of these
duties are significant.

71
As to the length of service, in his various
capacities, he was employed for 26 years from June, 1969 to August, 1995. This
is significant.

72
When the plaintiff was terminated he was
about 59 years of age.

73
The evidence supports a finding that there
were many advertisements for similar employment for persons with the
experience, training and qualifications of the plaintiff, however, not in the
Niagara Region and probably not for a person of the plaintiff’s age. I am of
the view that he faces a restricted prospect of future employment.

74
He did find some work as a Rabbi and a
Teacher in 1996.

75
The factors listed in
Bardal

are not
exhaustive.

76
There was an imbalance of the powers evident
here. The plaintiff trusted his employer to act fairly. He felt they had common
interests. The defendant prepared documents and the plaintiff signed them
without close scrutiny as to the period of employment. The plaintiff was
vulnerable under the circumstances. Eventually the defendant tried to
unilaterally exercise its power by relying on a term in a document which it
alleged to be in its favour. This is not acceptable.

77
Looking at all of the evidence I find that on
the balance of probabilities both parties considered the plaintiff to be a long
term employee and could stay as long as he wished subject to reasonable notice.
This in my view is an important factor in determining the notice period.

78
I find the defendant was not acting in good
faith when the plaintiff was handed the notice of termination letter dated
November 21, 1994 found at Exhibit 1, Tab 26. In view of my findings of how the
defendant supported and encouraged the plaintiff, they owed him the decency of
explaining why his contract would not be renewed. They did not. I find such
action detrimentally affected the sense of identity, self-worth, and emotional
well-being of the plaintiff.

79
I agree with counsel for the plaintiff that a
reasonable notice period at common law is 30 months to include the nine months
working notice.

80
(ii) What are the plaintiffs damages for
wrongful dismissal?

81
The plaintiff’s annual salary at the time of
dismissal was $65,000.00 or $5,416.66 per month. The gross damages are 30 times
$5,416.66 or $162,499.80. In 1995 he was paid $43,333.36 while he was working
for the defendant and in 1996 he earned $5,565.00 as a Rabbi and Teacher for
another employer for a total of $48,898.36. He did not earn any other income from
employment in the 30 month period. Neither the employment insurance benefits
nor the registered retirement savings plan income are to be deducted in
calculating damages. See Jorgenson v. Jack Cewe Ltd. (1980),
1980 CanLII 177 (SCC)
, 111 D.L.R. (3d)
577 (S.C.C.).

82
After deducting $48,898.36 from $162,499.80,
I arrive at $113,601.44. The plaintiff claims $110,000.00. I therefore award
damages for wrongful dismissal in the amount of $110,000.00 without further
amendment to the statement of claim.

83
(iii) Should the plaintiff’s damages for
wrongful dismissal be reduced on the basis that he failed to mitigate his
damages?

84
I find the plaintiff made all reasonable
efforts to mitigate his damages: I accept his evidence that the advertisements
for jobs entered as exhibits do not represent all of the jobs for which he
applied. He in fact did work in 1996 as a Rabbi and Teacher for which he was
paid. He tried his best to find employment.

85
C. Should the plaintiff be awarded punitive
damages and if so in what amount?

86
To decide this issue I must consider whether
there was an independent actionable wrong. See
Vorvis v. Insurance Corp. of
British Columbia
(1989),
1989 CanLII 93 (SCC)
, 25 C.C.E.L. 81 (S.C.C.) and
Wallace v.

United
Grain Growers Ltd.
(1997),
1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)
, 36 C.C.E.L. (2d) 1 (S.C.C).

87
Did the defendant’s conduct merit punishment?
Is this conduct exemplified by malice, fraud or cruelty as well as other
abusive and insolent acts toward the plaintiff. See page 103 of
Vorvis
referring
to
Warner v. Arsenault
(1982),
1982 CanLII 5380 (NS CA)
, 27 C.P.C. 200, 53 N.S.R. (2d) 146, 109
A.P.R. 146 (N.S. C.A.).

88
In
Robitaille v. Vancouver Hockey Club
Ltd.,
1981 CanLII 532 (BC CA)
, [1981] 3 W.W.R. 481 (B.C. C.A.) the punitive damages were ordered
because of the offensive attitude and conduct of the defendant
before
the
final injury occurred, (emphasis added).

89
It is argued by the defendant here that the
offensive conduct must be at the time of dismissal. I do not agree that the
Wallace

case goes that far. I am of the view that the actionable conduct in a
wrongful dismissal action can either lead up to or follow the act of dismissal
to be truly independent, provided that the court is satisfied that the strength
of the law must be vindicated and it must be demonstrated to the defendant that
the law will not tolerate conduct which wilfully disregards the rights of others.

90
Punitive damages ought to be awarded here. I
condemn the following conduct for being cruel, abusive, insolent and hurtful to
the plaintiff.

91
Even though the defendant provided the
plaintiff with the glowing letter found at Exhibit 1, Tab 28, extolling the
integrity, religious commitment and honour of the plaintiff, it instructed its
counsel to plead cause and set out particulars of cause found at page 21 of the
trial record. I find the particulars are unfounded and were eventually
withdrawn on the eve of trial. They were a personal attack on the plaintiff and
his family to hurt them. To add to this the defendant dismissed the plaintiff’s
wife to exacerbate the hurt to the plaintiff.

92
I find Exhibit 5 is a letter dated June 28,
1996 signed by David D. Cooperman, President of the Board of Governors,
calculated to put the plaintiff in a bad light for trying to enforce his rights
in the civil courts. Mr. Cooperman was not called to give evidence. There
was no evidence that he was unavailable. There was no explanation given by
Mr. Cooperman as to the purpose of the letter and therefore I draw the
adverse inference that he would not disagree that the purpose was to put down
the plaintiff in the eyes of the members of the Congregation.

93
The plaintiff was told by Mr. Cooperman
that he was no longer welcome in the Synagogue. Mr. Cooperman was not
called to deny this. I find that he in fact said this to the plaintiff and that
such conduct is malicious.

94
Finally, during the Festival of Sukkot, the
plaintiff and his son were treated in a most cruel and insolent manner when
they came to worship at the Synagogue. There were nine adult men present and
with the plaintiff and his son, a “
mynian
”

was present so that
the service began only to be stopped by a member of the defendant. I accept the
plaintiff’s explanation that the reason for this was that he and his son were
not being recognized for the purpose of constituting a “
mynian
”. I find
this conduct to be malicious as well. It must be remembered that this was the only
Synagogue in St. Catharines where the plaintiff could worship.
Mr. Williams, who gave evidence for the defendant, agreed that this
conduct produced a very serious result. 95 I fix punitive damages at
$20,000.00.

96 I find that the compensatory damages will not
suffice to achieve the goals of punishment and deterrence under the
circumstances.

7. Conclusion

97
There will be judgment for the plaintiff as follows:

(a) Damages for wrongful dismissal             -           $110,000.00

(b) Punitive Damages             -           20,000.00

8. Prejudgment Interest and Costs

98 Counsel may make submissions, in writing of
no more than five pages on a schedule to be agreed upon between them, the last
submission to be received by me no later than 20 days from today.

9. Addendum

99 In a letter dated March 17, 1999,
Mr. Grosman sent me a copy of the reasons of Mr. Justice Pitt in
Ceccol
v. Ontario Gymnastic Federation,
released February 15, 1999 [reported
(1999), 99 C.L.L.C. 210-014 (Ont. Gen. Div.)]. Mr. Donegan took exception
to this because time for delivery of submissions had expired.

100 I want counsel to know that I requested a
copy of the reasons from the office of Mr. Justice Pitt and received them
on February 23, 1999.

Action granted.

(Ont. Gen. Div.).
